Mr. Speaker, this week Susan Shoes Industries of Hamilton announced that it will be closing its Oakville plant permanently and that it will be laying off 100 employees. The reason for this plant closing is directly linked to the Mulroney Government's failure to state its position on the issue of import quotas. Shoe retailers will not place their orders for shoes because they are waiting to hear on the quota issue.
Once again the Government is called upon to stop playing cat and mouse with the Canadian footwear industry and to start making clear, positive statements ensuring that import quotas will be extended.
The removal of footwear quotas could cost 20,000 Canadian jobs in the footwear and tanning industries. Not only will thousands of Canadians be deprived of their livelihood, but they will also be forced to seek unemployment insurance and welfare assistance.
The Government has launched a so-called discussion with the United States on the issue of free trade, but in the meantime it has left Canadians hanging by footdragging on the issue of the shoe quotas.
A commitment by the Prime Minister (Mr. Mulroney) and the Minister of Regional Industrial Expansion (Mr. Stevens) to extend import quotas is essential to ensure that Canadian shoe manufacturers, like Susan Shoes, and, most important, Canadian workers, will have the time necessary for technological adjustment to secure 50 per cent of the market.
Job, jobs, jobs. We are giving the Prime Minister a chance, chance, chance to save 20,000 jobs in the footwear industry, and we call upon him to make his announcement today.

Mr. Speaker, once again Dr. Henry Morgantaler is facing the courts because of his attempt to demonstrate that women who so choose should have access to safe, medical abortions through community clinics as well as hospitals.
How long must these trials, appeals and retrials go on before the federal Government accepts that the real issue is not Dr. Henry Morgantaler's clinics but the need for changes to the Criminal Code of Canada? Section 251 must be repealed.
Difficult decisions about unwanted pregnancies must be a personal, not a state matter. Abortion should be a health matter between a woman and her doctor. Further restrictions of access will only lead to backstreet abortions.
Prevention of unwanted pregnancies is far preferable to abortion. Prevention requires reliable, safe birth control methods and comprehensive birth control education.
The Government must reinstate full funding to recognize family planning agencies which provide complete information on all methods of birth control. These agencies are doing research on fertility problems and more reliable birth control methods. Reproductive freedom for women is an integral part of equality. We ask the Government to repeal Section 251 and reinstate adequate funding to family planning organizations.

subsubtopic: EXPRESSION OF GOOD WISHES TO NEW QUEBEC PREMIER, HON. PIERRE-MARC JOHNSON
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I would like to take a few moments-and I am sure all my Quebec colleagues in the House will join me-to welcome the new Premier of Quebec, Mr. Pierre-Marc Johnson, who took up his duties officially yesterday morning at 11 o'clock, and wish him good luck. He is the twenty-fourth Premier of the province of Quebec.
Mr. Speaker, no one can deny the outstanding intellectual qualifications and leadership skills of Mr. Johnson, and his strong personality and capacity for hard work. Today's successor to Rene Levesque is not a newcomer to politics. Mr. Johnson was elected to the National Assembly for the first time in 1976, in the riding of Anjou, and re-elected in 1981. Since then, he has been Minister in a number of important departments, and, until his election as leader, he was Minister of Justice and the Minister responsible for Canadian Intergovernmental Affairs.
Mr. Speaker, the reins of power in Quebec have now been handed over to a man with broad political experience. I am sure he will represent and defend the interests of Quebecers with great dignity like his predecessor. I am sure that like Mr. Levesque, who had agreed to resume a dialogue with our Government, he will continue to work towards national reconciliation, in the best interests of Quebec and Canada.

Mr. Speaker, the Minister of Indian Affairs and Northern Development (Mr. Crombie) informed us yesterday that his Government will be going forward with a sweeping reorganization of the entire Indian Affairs Department. Some sources have suggested that this could mean a reduction of 1,500 jobs.
Yesterday in the House the Minister said that in so far as it relates to gathering the opinions of Indian people, he spent 14 months doing just that, and that he talked to every community.
This morning I spoke with the President of the Union of New Brunswick Indians, and I was informed that they were not consulted and that no other Indian groups from New Brunswick or the other maritime provinces were consulted. Therefore, it is evident that the Minister has not consulted with every Indian community and that, in my opinion, he misled the House.
I wish to remind the Minister that on April 18, in a statement regarding the development of aboriginal policy, the Prime Minister (Mr. Mulroney) said the following:
Policies regarding aboriginal people will be made after open, public consultation, especially at the grass roots level.
Evidently the directives of the Prime Minister are not being followed. Therefore, I implore the Government to respect its commitment and meet with all aboriginal groups.

Mr. Speaker, the philosophy of the Government that all public inspection and testing services should be carried out by private enterprise continues to get Canada in trouble. Today's case in point is the record of performance testing done on Canada's dairy cattle, known as ROP. The production and butterfat figures have been relied upon for years by foreign buyers in selecting our dairy breeding stock. They used to be an accurate reflection of the productive capabilities of the offspring of test animals.
The private testing program is not working. Samples are no longer tested on site but are carried for several days before the tests are completed. Perhaps the technicians have not yet properly learned their jobs. At any rate, results are extremely erratic, yet these results go on the production record for posterity. There is no notation that the result is probably in error due to testing procedure. The conclusion, therefore, by potential foreign buyers will be simply to avoid Canadian stock.
October 4, 1985

Further damage to our sales reputation must be avoided and corrected. As soon as the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Wise) returns from his trip to Russia, he must reverse this dismal decision to privatize ROP testing and get back to a professional program which will reflect the quality of our herds with accuracy. It is in the interest of all Canadians that trade continues in breeding stock. Surely it makes sense that we maintain the high standards needed for it to continue doing so.

subtopic: EXPORT EARNINGS-SUPPORT FOR CANADA-UNITED STATES NEGOTIATIONS
EXPORT EARNINGS-SUPPORT FOR CANADA-UNITED STATES NEGOTIATIONS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, few nations in the world are as dependent upon international trade as is Canada. The fact is that out of every dollar we earn in Canada, 30 cents result directly from exports. That figure would be higher if our trade performance were better, because every billion dollars in exports translates into nearly 16,000 jobs. The issue of bilateral trade is about jobs. Trade liberalization would create more jobs on both sides of the border.
Canada's most urgent need is for the creation of more jobs. What the critics of trade liberalization have consistently failed to realize is that Canadian firms and employees had to make even larger adjustments to the Kennedy and Tokyo Rounds of tariff cuts, yet the economy grew and employment increased. I need not emphasize the dramatic effect an additional 16,000 jobs would have on our unemployed. It is time that we gave our unemployed a fair chance.
A study by Queen's University has shown that employment in Canada would rise by 5 per cent because of increased trade access. The status quo is an option that just does not exist for Canada. The negotiated decision to be made by this Government is of the most strategic importance for all Canada. It will be one of the most important means of making the structural changes required for the security of our nation.

Mr. Speaker, I should like to congratulate our Government on steps taken to date in correcting a great disservice done to Canadians by the previous Government and its good friends, the NDP.
Although it is generally recognized that there are four fundamental human freedoms, the last Liberal Government saw fit to include only three of them in the Canadian Charter of Rights and Freedoms. The fourth, the right to enjoyment of property, was deliberately excluded from the Charter. This is all the more atrocious when one considers that the right to property was entrenched in the Diefenbaker Bill of Rights, but slashed from the Trudeau Charter of Rights. It is a strange

kind of Charter that ignores one of the fundamental human freedoms. Also it is a strange kind of Government that would adopt a seriously flawed Charter while proclaiming that Canadians would be forever protected because all their rights were now enshrined.

Even more significantly, Canadians will be seeking to preserve their rights to property. It is a week to celebrate property ownership. Our Government has given Canadians further cause to celebrate by initiating the process of entrenching property rights in the Charter.

Mr. Speaker, the Canadian Jobs Strategy is designed to meet the needs of those who are most in need, particularly older workers.
For example, in the job development program, long-term unemployed-many of whom are older workers-will be given training and employment opportunities in fields where they have not had any previous expertise. speakerposition: President of the Privy Council; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
speechtext: that Bill C-76, an Act respecting the operation of the Toronto Island Airport by the Toronto Harbour Commissioners, be read the second time and referred to a legislative committee.

speakeroldname: Hon. Perrin Beatty (Solicitor General of Canada):
speakerposition: Solicitor General of Canada
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, it appears to be my lucky day.

speakerposition: President of the Privy Council; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
speechtext: It is our lucky day.

speakerposition: Solicitor General of Canada
speechtext:
As the Government House Leader says as he leaves, it is our lucky day.
I want to make a few brief comments in the name of the Minister of Transport (Mr. Mazankowski) with regard to Bill C-76.

Mr. Speaker, the Toronto Island Airport is located in the Toronto Harbour area, about two miles from City Hall, on a property owned by the Toronto Harbour Commissioners, the City of Toronto and the federal Government. It has been designated as an airport to relieve pressure on Pearson International Airport. It serves a large general aviation community and a number of commercial aviation enterprises. It is also a STOL terminal for DASH-7 and DASH-8 aircraft.

In 1984-85, traffic at Toronto Island Airport reached over
156.000	aircraft movements and approximately 47,000 passengers. By the end of the decade, it is forecast that these figures will increase to about 200,000 aircraft movements and over
200.000	passengers. It was in recognition of the importance of Toronto Island Airport to the Toronto area aviation system that the federal Government entered into a 50-year lease agreement in June, 1983, with the City of Toronto and the Toronto Harbour Commissioners. In signing this lease agreement, the federal Government has ensured that the Toronto Island Airport will continue as an important airport in the Toronto area for general aviation and STOL services.
By way of background for the proposed amendments, I might say that Toronto Island Airport, until June 30, 1983, was operated under a lease agreement between the Toronto Harbour Commissioners and the City of Toronto. That lease expired on June 30, 1983, and in the absence of a new agreement, the Island Airport could have closed, causing severe congestion problems for other airports in the Toronto area, particularly for Pearson International.
Negotiations for a new agreement for the airport were long and protracted, primarily because of the environmental concerns of the City of Toronto with respect to air operations that would be allowed at the airport. Through the patience and understanding of all parties, a new lease was successfully

October 4, 1985
Toronto Island Airport
negotiated with ensured continued use of the site for airport purposes. However, it contains certain conditions which were requested by the city to address its environmental concerns with respect to operations at the airport and a need to preserve the integrity of neighbouring parkland. The former Minister of Transport, on behalf of the federal Government, agreed to recommend to Parliament amendments to the Toronto Harbour Commissioners Act to give effect to these conditions. Specifically, the city insisted that all jet aircraft and aircraft generating excessive noise, as defined in the lease, be prohibited from operating at the airport as a prerequisite to the city agreeing to enter into a long-term lease.
The amendments before the House are designed to provide statutory authority to allow the Toronto Harbour Commissioners to make by-laws to prohibit jet-powered aircraft and aircraft generating excessive noise, as defined in the lease, from operating at the airport, and will provide for a maximum fine of $25,000 upon summary conviction for owners of prohibited aircraft who use such aircraft at the airport.
It should be noted that although the proposed amendments appear to give discretionary power to the Toronto Harbour Commissioners to make the by-laws which I mentioned previously, under terms of the lease arrangement for Toronto Island Airport, the operator of the airport is obligated under Section 15(2) of the lease to make these by-laws and to enforce them strictly.
A further amendment requested by the City of Toronto concerning the operation of the airport is also addressed in the Bill. At the present time, under Section 7 of the Toronto Harbour Commissioners Act, 1911, the Island Airport is operated by the Toronto Harbour Commissioners on behalf of the City of Toronto. The city no longer wishes to be involved in the operation of the airport and wants to be indemnified against any financial or legal liability for the airport. Accordingly, an amendment is proposed to allow the Toronto Harbour Commissioners to operate the airport on its own behalf or, following agreement between the commissioners and the Minister of Transport, on behalf of Transport Canada.
It is intended that the Toronto Harbour Commissioners would in future operate the airport on behalf of Transport Canada. This would not increase federal Government expenditures because Transport Canada already funds all operating deficits and capital expenditures incurred by the Island Airport. In 1984, for example, the operating subsidy provided by the federal Government was about $475,000.
An additional amendment is also proposed concerning the appointment of commissioners by the City of Toronto to the Toronto Harbour Commissioners. Currently the city appoints three of the five members to the commission. The federal Government appoints the two other members, one being on the recommendation of the Metro Toronto Board of Trade. At present, the city appointments require nomination by the city's executive committee. The amendment will allow for members to be appointed by the majority of the Toronto City Council, without nomination by the executive committee. This amendment will bring the city's commissioner appointment process
into line with city appointments for other agencies and commissions.

Finally, Mr. Speaker, the purpose of these amendments is to make the Toronto Harbour Commissioners Act consistent with the Canadian Charter of Rights and Freedoms.
In concluding, I would like to point out that these amendments are being proposed in order to fulfil the federal Government's obligation under the lease for the Toronto Island Airport. The amendments are fundamental to the implementation of the specific terms of the lease, were prepared in consultation with the City of Toronto and the Toronto Harbour Commissioners, and have their support.
Signing a long-term lease ensures the continued use of the airport for general aviation and STOL operations. In turn, these operations benefit users of the air transportation network of Southern Ontario. Furthermore, they have and will continue to have a favourable impact on the economy of the Toronto urban area.

Mr. Speaker, my intervention will be a short one. I thank the Solicitor General (Mr. Beatty) for giving us such an interesting statistical description of the activities on Toronto Island emanating from the airport, as well as the history of this legislation and the economic considerations which he put before us.
In analysing this Bill it is important to keep in mind that there is more than just economic wellbeing, as described by the Minister, at stake here. There is also a very important set of islands that provide citizens with amenities and most enjoyable recreational outlets. In addition to that, the islands also provide, from an environmental point of view, a very important place of rest for migratory birds. Therefore, there are environmental as well as economic considerations that have to be taken into account.
In analysing this Bill it seems to me it would be desirable to produce a piece of legislation that will also have the input of interested individuals, groups of citizens, environmentalists, sailing and boating clubs as well as the groups already referred to by the Minister. It is my impression that the consultation process that has led to Bill C-76, an Act respecting the operation of the Toronto Island Airport by the Toronto Harbour Commission, requires a much broader base of consultation than has been given it so far. The Minister has already alluded to consultations with the City of Toronto, which is of course desirable and which we support. It seems to me that, once the Bill has been given second reading, a process of consultation ought to be launched by the committee to permit local consultations which so far have not taken place.
I would urge the Minister of Transport (Mr. Mazankowski) through the Solicitor General to permit the Transport Committee to hold hearings in metro Toronto so as to hear from
October 4, 1985

interested individuals and groups and, as I mentioned, environmentalist groups among them, sailing and boating clubs and the like.
It is important to remember that the islands are more than just a landing and take-off strip for transport purposes. This is a beautiful set of islands which have at one extreme, on Ward Island, a healthy and thriving community of homes and families. There is a set of parks that covers the balance of the area and the airport activities, large in number as they are-I was surprised to hear the Minister referring to 156,000 aircraft movements-representing in terms of land use only a small fraction of the totality of what these islands are all about. From the point of view of Toronto citizens, the islands mean much more than just aircraft movements.
The powers given to the commissioners in this Bill seem to me to be too sweeping. Looking at the expropriation powers outlined in Section 7 it seems to me that the commissioners, if given the opportunity, would have expropriation powers that are unusually strong without any provision for appeal that I was able to detect in the Bill. Therefore, I would like to draw the attention of the Minister to the necessity of introducing in the Bill a mechanism for individuals, clubs, environmentalist groups or whoever has some kind of activity on the island that would be endangered by a process of expropriation to have a recourse-and I know that the Solicitor General is very keen and well versed and has had considerable experience-

speakerposition: Solicitor General of Canada
speechtext: You are trying to flatter me into something.

-an avenue for appealing to the powers established under any piece of legislation. It is important that an appeal process be provided, when one thinks not just of tomorrow or five years from now but of future generations of Canadians and Torontonians who enjoy very much the use of the islands for recreational purposes.
Under Section 7 there are power being outlined that may be given to the commission for the use of jet-powered aircraft. I urge the Government to reconsider the possibility envisaged in this Bill to permit jet-powered aircraft. We have Malton; we have excellent facilities at the Lester B. Pearson Airport. There is no need in the downtown area to expand the activities of that airport to include jets.
The reason for that will become more evident when we talk about the island as an area being used by migratory birds.
The section that permits commissioners to deal with levels of noise leaves me a little bit puzzled because I do not know what the definition of the words "excessive levels of noise" will be. Will it be the levels of noise as defined and applied by the City of Toronto under its present by-laws, or will it be a definition that the commissioners will develop on their own and, if so, will they do it in consultation with the city? As we all know, words like "excessive", are very hard to define when it comes to the practical application of a proposed piece of legislation. I would be grateful if the Solicitor General or the Minister of Transport would come back and explain to us how in the term "excessive levels of noise", the word "excessive" is to be applied in practice.
Toronto Island Airport
In Section 10 there is phraseoly which I suppose is quite common and I would not want to be misunderstood in trying to pick every detail out of this Bill. But it seems to me that wherever the words "his successor" are used, as on the last line of page 4, the implication is that only male commissioners would be appointed. I think that as the general practice from now on, for all the good reasons that we know, the drafters of the Bill should insert the words "his or her successor" and thus give the fullest opportunity to interpret the full meaning of what the legislators had in mind.
The general picture that emerges from this Bill is one that 1 look at with a bit of concern. We are considering the commissioners regulating air traffic and airport activities in dowtown Toronto. This is an increasingly heavily built up area. We have the CN Tower, several hotels and a number of existing high-rise buildings. More will follow if existing plans are carried out. Therefore, it seems to me that caution should be used here in looking at the future use of this airport. That is why the reference is made to the undesirability of permitting jet aircraft traffic.
I would like to raise a question on which the Minister of Transport may wish to comment at the end of the debate. At this airport, do we have the latest and most adequate radar facilities to assist and permit flights in bad weather? In the winter months and when visibility becomes difficult, this airport must be equipped with the best and latest facilities that exist in larger airports. We cannot afford to take any risks at all.
This Bill does not have an environmental clause, and it seems to me that a word or two is needed on the migration of birds. In the area, I am told that there is an intensive activity from North to South and vice versa in the appropriate migration seasons. The islands are considered to be a green oasis for all species of birds existing in our climate and others. Some 250 species of birds have been counted over a year and easily several million individual birds have been counted annually.
Lake Ontario has a habitat different from the neighbouring Great Lakes and therefore the type of bird migration that we see here on the island has a unique characteristic that must be kept in mind and protected. This area is the only place in Metro Toronto where certain types of birds can be observed by naturalists, school children and those interested in wildlife and nature. In fact, on Toronto Island there is a unique school with a fine and ancient tradition of outdoor education. At every time of year possible, children are taken there for a full week in order to carry on nature studies on site.
We have in this area a stopover point for migrating birds. We have a nesting place and an area in which birds live year round. Therefore, we have a natural asset that must be taken into account whenever we begin to talk about aircraft activity. In conclusion, since we are talking about powers being transferred by the city to the commissioners, what is missing in this Bill is that the commissioners should have the power to close the island airport for any number of days required during the

October 4, 1985
Toronto Island Airport
critical migration time of the birds if and when this seems to be desirable and required. I welcome the opportunity to have the ear of the Solicitor General during this intervention. I know that he will take to heart the points that are being made. I know that he is a very keen, devoted and committed environmentalist and I know that he is particularly keen about the protection of the migration paths of birds. Therefore, we will have in him a champion for the cause of Toronto Island which, as I said, is much more than a place in which to put an airport. It is a very important recreational and environmental part of Metro-Toronto, something which makes Metro-Toronto such an admired city the world over.

Mr. Speaker, as transportation critic for my Party, I am happy to rise to speak on this Bill. First, I wish to express my appreciation to my colleague, the Hon. Member for Spadina (Mr. Heap), for allowing me to speak before he does. Although this airport is located in his constituency, he has been good enough to let me speak first so that I can leave town later this afternoon.
I have a question of the Solicitor General (Mr. Beatty). What the heck is he doing introducing this Bill? In all my years here, the Minister of Transport or at times even his Parliamentary Secretary led off any debate on transportation. Why did the Minister of State for Transport (Mrs. Blais-Grenier) not lead off this debate in the justifiable absence of the Minister of Transport (Mr. Mazankowski)? I do not understand it. Is it because the Minister of State for Transport is being relieved of her duties by the back door because of other events and other situations? Is the Minister of State for Transport being hidden from Parliament and prevented from carrying out her responsibilities? It is a question I hope a subsequent speaker from the Government side will answer.

speakerposition: Solicitor General of Canada
speechtext: No, it's because I was desperate to speak to this Bill, Les.
I appreciated the remarks of the Hon. Member for Davenport (Mr. Caccia). However, I would remind him that it was the Liberals who started all this.
Started what?

I would remind him that it was three successive Liberal Ministers of Transport who promoted and encouraged STOL aircraft service and who supported the expansion and increased use of the Toronto Island Airport. Now the Tories are doing the same thing in spades. I think the Hon. Member for Davenport should have made the speech he made today on the numerous opportunities he would have had over the last number of years.
This is the first time this Bill has been introduced.

The Hon. Member for Davenport and anyone else who was on the Government side when the Liberals were in power could have spoken on this matter in a Throne Speech debate or a budget debate. They could have raised hell
in the debate on the Estimates. They could have said a lot of things. It is amazing how their tunes change when the two old Parties change places.
It is too bad that we did not have more time to look into the ramifications of this little Bill because they go far beyond what is contained in it. For many years, the operation of this airport has created a controversy on the Toronto waterfront, the Toronto City Council and among citizens of Toronto in general. My colleague, the Hon. Member for Spadina, who is also a former member of the city council for the area, will probably fill us in on some of the history of the development of the Toronto Island in general and the airport in particular. He shall undoubtedly let us know about the not-so-glorious history of the Toronto Harbour Commission as well. I leave that to him to do as I know he will do so very well.
It is too bad the Government wants to put this Bill through. The debate on this matter has been going on for some time, not only in the context of the Toronto Island Airport and the short take-off and landing services but in the context of how the Government of the day works at cross purposes. Regarding Via Rail, the Government has invested tens of millions of dollars in a high-speed passenger train called the LRC in order to provide a high speed, frequent and efficient service in the Quebec City-Montreal-Ottawa-Toronto-Windsor corridor. It has made this investment to attract people away from their automobiles and, hopefully, out of some of the congested airports in order to provide a service which a large number of people want. That is fine. Then, what does the Government do? At the same time, through the provision of capital, it proceeds to make way for the operations of a short take-off and landing aircraft service in the same corridor. That move can do nothing but inhibit, if not decrease, the potential for passenger increases on VIA Rail.
When the Government sinks a few hundred million dollars into some 31 locomotives and, I believe, something in the order of 150 passenger cars for the LRC, and then at the same time turns around and spends money to provide an additional service, even though there are lots of buses, trains and other aircraft operating in the same corridor, it seems to defeat the original purpose. I do not see the Toronto Harbour Commission having the money to spend on this measure since, as far as I know, the commission does not have any money. I do not understand.
I criticized the previous Liberal Government for working at cross purposes within its own ranks. 1 thought we would see some change on the part of the new Conservative Government. I'll be darned if it is not doing exactly the same thing. It is incredible. There were Conservatives who stood up as often as we did in previous years to criticize what the Liberals were attempting to do with respect to the Toronto Island Airport and the whole matter of short take-off and landing services in the Quebec-Windsor corridor, including Montreal, Ottawa and Toronto.
October 4, 1985

The place for that type of service is not in a highly populated and congested area where there are numerous other services such as super-highways, eight or ten buses a day, four or five airlines operating flights and VIA Rail's operations. What does the Government do? It inserts another service which divides the market up into even smaller pieces. People participating in the market take turns at going broke and the taxpayers pick up the tab. I do not understand it.
The place for short take-off and landing aircraft is not on expensive runways with expensive infrastructures. The place for this type of service is in sparseley populated areas in the northern parts of our provinces and in Arctic Canada. Short take-off and landing aircraft can be used on a gravel strip if need be. Low cost and frequent service can be provided, and those are the places for that type of aircraft.
I understand and appreciate that the Government is anxious with respect to the sale of Dash-7s and Dash-8s. I understand the Government is trying to entice countries such as Brazil, Argentina, other South American countries in the Andes Mountains such as Chile, Peru and Bolivia, as well as some European countries, to buy short take-off and landing aircraft, which are darned good aircraft. Those countries have large isolated areas and widely scattered populations where the use of that type of aircraft is ideal, such as in the jungles of Brazil, the prairies of the Argentine or the mountains of western South America.
We were told by the bureaucrats and the Government of the day a few years ago that this short take-off and landing service out of Toronto Island Airport would serve as a demonstration model for potential buyers. Well, the potential buyers received all types of demonstration models out of metropolitan areas all over the world and had the experience of probably 100 different airlines to draw from. Canada had a golden opportunity to make a much better and proper use of short take-off and landing aircraft for a demonstration model in order to entice other countries to buy those aircraft. Instead of doing that, the Government is setting up an elitist air service for business executives, corporate directors and MPs. I do not know of many pensioners or low income people who will be able to use the service.
Thus, the Government has done it backward again. From the content of the Bill, we are not sure what the Government plans for the work of the Toronto Harbour Commission. In fact, members of the New Democratic Party are not sure what the intentions of the harbour commission are toward the future of the airport. We are not convinced it will keep jets out of the airport in accordance with its agreement with the City of Toronto. The Bill states that the Toronto Harbour Commission may prohibit the use of jets. All that means is that if the commission does not say anything, then someone else can use jets. That is all that means. It seems to me the Government had better make up its mind since there is an agreement between the City of Toronto and the Toronto Harbour Commission. Is the Government trying to undermine the City of Toronto and undermine the agreement and allow the harbour commission to do whatever it likes? We are not sure the
Toronto Island Airport
harbour commission will not use the powers of expropriation which it will be given by this Bill to obtain the lands it needs to build the bridge it wants, to expand its terminal and runway to accommodate larger and, perhaps, jet-powered aircraft at the Toronto Island Airport.
I can recall a time when the Transport Committee visited the Toronto Island Airport. It was a boar's nest. What passes for a terminal there would not make a good granary on the Prairies. The best thing that could happen to it would be a fire.

speakerposition: Minister of State (Immigration)
speechtext: Good Lord, an arsonist!

Obviously, what will have to happen if, as and when this Bill passes, will be the building of a new terminal. More and larger fire and emergency services will have to be put in place. The airport will need more land. The City of Toronto and the residents of Toronto Island have been most vociferous, with some justification, about the preservation of the parks, the nice residences and the milieu in which they live on Toronto Island. They can kiss all that good-bye since there is no doubt the move is eventually to have a major airport operation in the Toronto harbour compared to what is in place now.
I cannot understand that the hell a harbour commission is doing running an airport. However, if it can improve matters then I wonder if we can have a harbour commission in Regina to run our airport and perhaps it could even run the international airport in Edmonton. It passes my understanding what the dickens a harbour commission is doing running an airport. I thought its concerns were with water and not air.
We feel these matters need to be cleared up before we can give support to the Minister's proposed changes. For example, Mr. Speaker, large co-op housing developments are being built only a short distance from that airport. That may cause those who are going to build, whether co-op housing or any other kind, to step back and take another look, because a few years down the road when this becomes something of a major metropolitan airport operation, they probably will not be able to give the development away.
At the moment, we are inclined to oppose this legislation and we want a lot of answers. We believe that this Bill should not only go to committee but we want a commitment from the Solicitor General, since he is in charge of this Bill at least for today, that the committee on Transport or the Legislative Committee will be authorized and empowered by an order of reference in this House to hold hearings in the City of Toronto. If that takes two or three days, that's fine, but hearings just in Ottawa will not be sufficient. There are too many people who are interested who cannot afford the travelling expense. The great thing about Toronto is that there are members of the New Democratic Party who are members of the Legislative Assembly, it has the Blue Jays, and my son, daughter-in-law and grandson live there. The New Democratic Party in the Prairies has a secret plan for Toronto-we just fill it full of wheat. There are some great people living there and

October 4, 1985
Toronto Island Airport
there is a nice park there which they want preserved. You can bet your bottom dollar, Mr. Speaker, that by the time these great Tory business types get through with that place in two or three years, some of those residents, if they do not sell out now, will not be able to get much for their property.
The Minister has proposed privatizing airports, which is something we do not generally support, although there is nothing new about provincially and municipally owned airports. We did not think, however, that he meant to give over the operation and the profits, if any, while retaining the responsibility for any potential loss. That is great Tory business sense, Mr. Speaker. If it makes money, business gets to keep it, and if it loses money, the taxpayers get to pay for it. They are marvellous businessmen. I am sure that this is a principle which would go over pretty well at the local Chamber of Commerce meeting. This is, of course, a standard procedure not only in this administration but in previous administrations as well. That's what happens when the tweedle-dees and the tweedle-dums are in charge. They involve themselves in business only when business needs the money.
Who is in this Toronto Harbour Commission which the Conservatives wish to put in charge of the Toronto Island Airport? The City Council gets to elect three of its members, and I suppose it is an improvement in the Bill that it will take a majority vote of the City Council and that any member of the Council can nominate a candidate for the position. I suppose that is a democratic improvement. However, why should the Toronto Board of Trade get to pick those fellows who run around in their yachting caps, blue blazers and grey flannels, the big wheels? How about the Toronto the District Labour Council or the residents' association in that area nominating someone to that harbour commission? This Government has bragged about being open and more democratic. Why should this body not be beefed up to include real elected representatives from City Council instead of a few nauticals types? Why not someone who lives on the island? No one will suffer greater change than the residents of the island community if a bridge or tunnel to link the islands were approved or built by the harbour commission.
Obviously, because the Minister has opened up the membership of the commission through this Bill even he recognizes that there should be some changes. I think we may have to move some amendments which will make a few more changes. I think we may have to move amendments which will make a few more changes.
I look on this, Mr. Speaker, as part of the whole "freedom to move" syndrome of the Government which wa started by the Liberals in 1974-1975 under the Hon. Otto Lang. It was user-pay, deregulation, too much Government, cut-backs, restraint; the "proposition 13" syndrome imported from California. It means, in the case of the Toronto Island Airport, freedom to change the different types of aircraft. It means new companies serving that airport with no need to justify their arrival, and they will want roads and warehouses and service centres and so on. It means more congestion and crowding on the island which is already congested. Getting there in a car is
enough to give a coyote heartburn, and this will make it even worse for the people who reside on that island. This will involve changes to the whole waterfront because of the change to the regulations of railroads and shipping which the Government proposes in its "freedom to move White Paper". In fact, the Toronto Island Airport Bill is only one of a whole host of relatively minor things in the total package which this Government, following the lead of the previous Government, wants to implement in Canada in order to impose a theory which is at best unproven and at worst, I submit, is proven to be bad transportation economics, bad for the public and bad for the taxpayers.	,
The experience in other places has not shown that the so-called "freedom to move" syndrome, which I call "freedom to manoeuvre", in fact will be any kind of an improvement except to a few of the big operators. They will have a ball, as usual. But the ordinary people who live in places like the Toronto Island, who cannot afford the luxury of flying on executive-type aircraft, are not being taken into consideration.
I submit that this Bill, Mr. Speaker, is just a continuation of a Government working at cross purposes when it invests in high speed rail passenger service and also invests in a competing mode of transportation which will take customers away from the rail service.
