speechtext:
that
In the opinion of this House, the Government should consider the advisability of supporting the textile industry by:
1.	using the provisions of section 19 of the General Agreement on Tariffs and
Trade to impose a global quota on the importation of textiles; and
2.	amending section 11 of the Labour Adjustment Benefits Act to extend the
program to layoffs which represent 10 per cent of the employees in a particular
branch or division of a company and not only to those layoffs involving at least
10 per cent or 50 employees of the total establishment.
He said: Mr. Speaker, thank you for putting my motion before the House. My purpose is to increase the Government's awareness of the situation in the textile and garment industry.
Mr. Speaker, this is an industry that I know and support, and I know what I am talking about because I spent thirteen years there. I also would like to take this opportunity to say a few words about my beautiful part of the country. The Saint-Fran?ois River flows across the entire breadth of the riding of Drummond, which is located a few kilometers south of the St. Lawrence River. It is situated between Montreal and Quebec City, if one takes the Trans-Canada Highway, and between Trois-Rivieres and Sherbrooke if one is travelling on Highway 55. The location of Drummond between these four cities puts it right in Quebec's heartland.
The riding has a population of 75,000, spread over 28 municipalities and an area of 1,675 square kilometers.
The majority of the population is francophone, but the cultural, social and economic contribution of various ethnic groups in the region is still significant.
An industrial profile of Drummond would not be complete without a reference to the textile industry, because in the past, the industry's contribution to the economy of the riding was a very important one. Nevertheless, companies such as Celanese, Dominion Textile, Consoltex, Textile Dionne, Teinture Elite and several other enterprises in Drummondville continue to provide a living for the people in this riding.
The total number of jobs that depend on the textile and garment industry in the riding exceeds 5,000, which shows that the industry is still responsible for the major part of the region's economy.
To illustrate the importance of an industry like Celanese in the Drummondville area, I can inform Hon. Members that this compagny generates a payroll of $25 million a year, that it pays $500,000 in taxes to the City of Drummondville, that it contributes over $100,000 per year through its budget for
7362

October 4, 1985
Textile Industry
social activities, and that furthermore, it has just spent over one million dollars converting its heating plant to natural gas. It has also just invested another million in two silos for storing chemical products used in manufacturing yarns.
Mr. Speaker, the purpose of the motion before the House is to provide some solutions to the problems of the textile and garment industry and to ensure its protection and survival. As we all know, jobs are being threatened by imports from the semi-industrialized countries of the Pacific Rim.
As evidence of this I would mention the numerous plant closures such as Wabasso last March and, quite recently, Dominion Textile's announcement concerning the shutdown of two plants in Beauharnois and Valleyfield, with the resulting loss of 850 jobs. According to company spokesmen, the main reason for closing those plants was the ever growing clothing imports from low wage countries.
Mr. Speaker, the number of imported clothing units was 160 million in 1981 as compared with 244 million last year. In fact, on a per capita basis we let in twice as many imports as the United States do.
It is obvious that rising imports far exceed Canada's economic growth. It is an increase of 45 per cent, whereas over the past five years the market has expanded by only 1.5 per cent a year, and it is now at the 540 million unit level.
Higher imports in the last ten years have led to 35,000 fewer jobs in Canada. In addition those imports now account for more than 60 per cent of our domestic market. American textile industries have an advantage because most manufacturing operations in foreign countries are done in American branch plants or by companies under their control in developing countries. The net result is that they improve their financial situation through profits from foreign operations.
Mr. Speaker, I would like to give a few examples of countries which did not hesitate to come to the rescue of their industries. Over the past 15 years the Japanese have intervened directly in that sector to prevent the decline of their industries, and their annual textile and clothing imports have gone up by only 2 per cent. Think about it, Mr. Speaker, 2 per cent in Japan against a 45 per cent increase in four years in Canada. Many Japanese textile manufacturers have moved their operations to Southeast Asia where labour is cheap. Those manufacturers can then ship their exports through other Asian countries. Mr. Speaker, I would like to give you more examples about the Japanese. Here, from Global Textile Industries Figure 48, Annex 7: preferential financing at interest rates of 2.6 to 7.6 per cent for ten years; unit production costs financed by the national Government to the tune of 50 to 70 per cent, not to mention deferred payments, grants and what have you. And then Figure 52 reveals that Japanese companies have set up shop in various countries of Western Asia, such as Taiwan where they have 47 plants or industries,
Hong Kong with 18, Korea with 47, Thailand with 32, and so on down the list.
There is also the European Economic Community, or EEC, also called the Common Market, which includes 13 European countries. Their per capita textile imports have gone down from $11.80 in 1980 to $8.30 in 1984 and their clothing imports from $22.30 in 1980 to $18.40 in 1984. Incidentally, during the Multifibre Arrangements III negotiations, the EEC asked for more restrictions on imports. They proposed a 1 per cent increase and advised the European Commissioner that they would take unilateral action if other countries refused their proposals. Both the industries and the unions agreed to ask for better protection against low cost suppliers. The employers and the unions found a 6 per cent rate increase for imports excessive in view of an estimated yearly market increase of between 1 and 1.5 per cent and demanded that the rate of increase for imports be lower than the rate of increase of the market to allow European businesses to make some slight progress. The unions also suggested that the EEC fine the member countries which would authorize imports in excess of their quotas and that unused parts of quotas no longer be carried over or transferred.
Imports from the main suppliers were to decrease by 10 percent over five years. The mechanism to prevent sudden increases and designed to stop an excessive inflow of imports, whatever the level of quotas, was agreed to at the same time as arrangements for an anti-fraud clause.
Mr. Speaker, this information comes from an article published in the autumn 1983 issue of the periodical International Organization.
Certain countries try to get around the rules of the MFA. For instance, Hong Kong buys and sells used quotas from other countries. Another means is to use a third country which does not have any quota agreement. For example, Mr. Speaker, the allocation cost for selling a quota for a pair of jeans was 55 per cent of the allocation price of these same jeans.
We can see that most textile and clothing producing countries provide assistance of various types to their own industries.
Through the CIRB, the federal Government has granted subsidies of $108 million and $70 million respectively to the textile and clothing industries. During the last 10 years, the textile industry has invested $2.4 billion to modernize its equipment. Incidentally, the federal Members of Parliament had an opportunity last August to visit the textile, clothing and shoe industries in Quebec and Ontario during a tour organized by the Minister of Regional Industrial Expansion (Mr. Stevens).
Like many EEC countries and semi-industrialized or developing countries, Canada must develop a federal textile and clothing policy as quickly as possile to determine the rules
October 4, 1985

of the game. Industries in these sectors in Canada are not asking for any subsidies. They want the Government to reduce the quotas and to give them a larger share of the domestic market.
Let me remind the House that the clothing industry is a very fragmented and labour-intensive industry and that between 24 and 40 cents out of every dollar produced by the sales of a clothing item go back to the worker. I think it would be difficult to find many other industrial sectors where the cost of creating one job is so low. On the other hand, the textile industry is very complex and capital-intensive. It costs at least $300,000 to create one job in this industry. Manpower costs represent only 15 percent of total costs. In addition, the western petro-chemical industry is dependent on the textile industry for $100 million in sales each year. This industry provides jobs for 75,100 people and the clothing industry gives employment to 99,000 workers in Canada. Also, it is estimated that 275,000 additional jobs in Canada are indirectly related to these industries.
Our industries have trouble competing against countries where wages are low and workers receive an hourly wage of between 21 cents and $1.50 an hour. This is why, Mr. Speaker, I am asking the Government to state its policies as soon as possible. The Multifibre Agreement was extended in 1977, and again in 1981. Each time, Sections 3 and 4 remained unchanged. In the 1977 Protocol extending the agreement, the parties thereto however allowed the possibility of jointly agreeing on reasonable temporary adjustments on specific points in given cases. The 1981 Protocol was worded in a more liberal way still, and it increased the extent to which importing countries could restrain importats under Sections 3 and 4.
The 1981 Protocol allowed importing countries to align their levels of importation on the domestic consumption growth rate, in order to determine market disruptions. Further, the Protocol enabled the parties to reach an understanding based on a level of positive growth lower than that provided for in Schedule B of the MFA in exceptional cases where there was a recurrence or intensification of market disruption. It also authorized any mutually acceptable agreement for reasons of flexibility in cases where the generous use of quotas with a very high level of restrictions represents an important share of the market. Finally, the 1981 Protocol provided for an "anti-increase" mechanism. It left the contracting parties quite free to negotiate agreements to resolve important difficulties arising from the repeated under-utilization of significant levels of restrictions that threaten to result in serious and real damage.
To that end, I have thought out a few scenarios. A 200 million unit per year quota would enable us to create 6,500 jobs more than in 1984. A 175 million unit quota would enable us to create 17,900 jobs in the textile and clothing industries.
Mr. Speaker, according to the Canadian textile industry, their share of the Canadian market has declined from 43 per cent in 1981 to 37 per cent in 1984. This is a good enough reason to invoke Section XIX of the GATT Agreement. They
Textile Industry
recognize that the increase in importation depresses activity in the primary textile industries which supply raw materials to the clothing industry. Further, it should be noted that the textile industry and the clothing industry are dependent on each other as it was emphasized in a study made in 1985 by the Quebec Department of Industry, Trade and Commerce.
Therefore, it is my view that the Government should impose an overall quota on imports from all sources under Section 19 of the GATT Agreement. Such action is self-explanatory, because when we negotiated the agreements we were not as tough as we should have been and our legitimate rights, as described in the Multifibre Agreement, have not been adequat-ly defended by the previous administration.
The use of Section 19 would abrogate the 21 bilateral agreements signed by Canada with fabric and clothing exporting countries. Those agreements would be replaced by an overall ceiling on clothing imports from all sources, whether from under-developed countries, newly industrialized nations or nations with state controlled or market-oriented economies.
The Government has to make sure that existing and future quota agreements are administered and negotiated by taking advantage of all the international rights Canada has under the Multifibre Agreement.
Such instruments are subject to the international rules grouped in the various GATT codes. Their legitimate use has nothing to do with protectionism. Within its jurisdiction and under the international agreements that were ratified, the Government has the right and the responsibility to do so.
This Government must develop a policy designed to provide leadership, to create a framework and conditions for development aimed at promoting a climate of confidence in which the industry will invest, and undertake or continue the manufacturing of competitive products.
Mr. Speaker, I would like to add a few words concerning the second part of the motion, which is designed to amend the legislation on manpower adjustment benefits, Chapter 89 of the Revised Statutes of Canada. In fact, Section 11(c), as now worded, is prejudicial in my view to certain workers in the textiles, clothing and shoe industries.
As it now stands, one of the requirements before employees are certified is that the number of employees in the plant has been reduced through lay-offs by at least 10 per cent or, if the reduction is lower than 10 per cent, by at least 50 employees.
Mr. Speaker, this is unfair for some of the workers because generally it is a branch or a department of the plant rather than the whole plant that is closed. This means that some workers cannot be registered under that legislation. We should not forget that this legislation comes under the Minister of Labour (Mr. McKnight) and its purpose is to protect older workers who have been permanently laid off in sectors of operations designated by the federal Government. They do not qualify for unemployment insurance benefits and they have no

October 4, 1985
Textile Industry
prospect of getting a job. Those benefits to be considered as a continuation of income are a last resort adjustment for older workers who on account of their age and their qualifications do not qualify for the manpower employment program and find it very difficult to cope with the new conditions.
The program is of valuable assistance to those who are more deeply affected by the shutdown of plants and the loss of jobs. It is an answer to some rather difficult conditions and helps people who have no other alternative. Moreover, Mr. Speaker, it does not apply to millions of people since, according to the most recent report from October 1st to December 31st, 1984, there were 198 applications for certification of which 150 only were approved and 48 were disallowed mainly for the above-mentioned reason.
Mr. Speaker, this amendment seems to me to be important and I ask the Government to act quickly since the shutdown of other plants in the textile, clothing and footwear industries has been announced.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I have listened very carefully to the remarks of the Hon. Member for Drummond (Mr. Guilbault). At the outset, as he launched into a description of his constituency, I started wondering if he was delivering the Address in reply to the Throne Speech. But I soon came to realize that in describing his constituency, he was in fact outlining how important the textile industry was in that area.
The textile industry, Mr. Speaker, is also very important for the constituency I represent. Now, in the western part of that constituency, as you get closer to the National Capital, textile industry nothing to write home about, but in the eastern part of my constituency, in cities like Alexandria, Hawkesbury, l'Original and others, that industry does play an important part. In the towns of Hawkesbury and Alexandria, and other town as well, we have textile plants such as Amoco, Consoltex, Fibre World, White Sister, Canadian Uniforms, Canadian Buttons, Texturon, Wonder Bra, and a few others-those manufacturers are going to be angry at me for not mentioning their names, but it was not intentional-we have a lot of those plants in my constituency, Mr. Speaker, and they bear heavily on the employment picture for my constituents.
The footwear industry also plays an important part in my constituency, and I feel it would be appropriate for me to dwell on that textile related subject for a minute or two this afternoon.
As everyone knows, footwear quotas will be lifted in a few weeks' time, on the 30th of November, and as the deadline looms, the Secretary of States for External Affairs (Mr. Clark) and his counterpart the Minister for International Trade still have made no statement to the House with respect to the footwear industry. This is most inappropriate as that industry employs 350 people in the Glengarry-Prescott-Russell constituency. Over the last few days, I have received 131
letters from employees asking for my help so that they don't get laid off as a result of this Conservative Government's carelessness, and I wish to take this opportunity to raise the matter in the House, as it is of utmost importance for my constituents.
Having said that, I will get back to the file on the textile industry itself, before you call me to order, Mr. Speaker, since the file on the footwear industry is similar but not quite the same. Let us say that ... Mr. Speaker, I do not want to interrupt those Conservative Members who are saying goodbye to everybody, but I would like to continue with my remarks.
In my riding, aside from the 350 jobs in the footwear industry which I have already mentioned, there are some 1,500 or 1,600 jobs in the textile industry. These too are very important for my constituents.
Mr. Speaker, I have here some letters from employees of textile companies in my riding who are asking my help so that they, too, can keep their jobs, which they feel are threatened by this Progressive Conservative Government's inaction. But I am pleased to see that some Progressive Conservative Members in this House share the view that the Government should do something to protect the jobs of the textile workers; I am pleased as well to know that the Hon. Member for Drummond (Mr. Guilbault) is among those who think that the Government should move and help people in his riding and within the whole industry.

Last summer during the election campaign, Mr. Speaker, the Conservative Party made a number of promises which 1 believe I may have raised with you once or twice previously. More particularly, it made a number of promises to the textile workers. I would like to read some of them to you, Mr. Speaker. The first promise was to "promote fair trade but not free trade". Would you believe that the Conservatives said that last summer, Mr. Speaker? Second, "promote stability through the rigorous enforcement of our existing international rights and obligations including, if necessary, the establishment of global quotas and a controlled increase of import volumes". That is a promise made by the Conservatives last summer. I know that the Hon. Member for Dollar (Mr. Weiner), who is listening attentively, has taken note of that particular promise which was made in Sherbrooke, would you believe, Mr. Speaker, by the Prime Minister (Mr. Mulroney), then Leader of the Conservative Party? I am sure that other Hon, Members might want to speak on this subject in the future and say whether or not they agree with promise No. 2 made by the Leader of the Conservative Party last summer. The third promise made by the Conservative Party, and again I read from the "Book of Promises", "review Canada's existing obligations in order to ascertain whether modifications should be pursued". A fourth promise was, "promote specialization in those areas with the best prospects for long-term economic viability". The fifth promise was, "promote the nationalization
October 4, 1985

of Canadian production through the use of duty remission schemes so that Canadian producers can work with low-cost foreign producers, combining Canadian expertise in fashion, marketing, and financial techniques with foreign products in pursuit of other markets in the world". That is a long-winded promise which I have read on a number of occasions and I am still not quite able to decipher what exactly it means except that it seems to contradict promise No. 2. Of course, that would not be the first time that Conservative promises were not consistent. The only consistency in Conservative promises has been the fact that they have been so inconsistent.
Promise No. 6 was to "promote the auctioning of import quotas in order to provide funds for the modernization of the industry". Promise No. 7 was to "decrease the use of grants".
I wonder how one would reconcile that with promise No. 4. However, Tories can sometimes rationalize these things. Promise No. 8 was to "increase the use of tax incentives to reward success, including the broadening of the tax definition of research and development". I remind you of promise No. 7, Mr. Speaker, which I read a few seconds ago. You can see how consistent that is. The ninth promise was to "promote the greater partipation by representatives of the industry in the formulation of textile and apparel policy". I will stop right here, Mr. Speaker, because 1 think it is important to discuss promise No. 9. As you recall, that promise talks about consultation with industry. 1 want to draw to your attention, Mr. Speaker, a letter written in December, 1984, by the Moderator of the Canadian Textile Labour-Management Committee of the Industrial Relations Department of the University of Laval in Quebec City to the Minister of Regional Industrial Expansion (Mr. Stevens). The Reverend pointed out that he had been trying to get a meeting with the Minister for six months and never could meet him. The promise was that the Conservative Party would consult with the textile industry. Yet, six months later, they did not have the time to meet with the people who had a lot to do with that industry. I think this could be interpreted by some as being inconsistent.

Mr. Speaker, I was getting rather apprehensive that perhaps I would not get a chance to speak. The Member seemed to be prepared to carry on for some time.
I should also remind the Member that there are people in my riding who would like to hear me make representations on their behalf. As well, I would like to make some comments for the record on behalf of the Department that I represent, the Department of Labour.
I want to begin by thanking and commending the Hon. Member for Drummond (Mr. Guilbault) for bringing to the floor of the House an issue that is indeed important to him and I know very important to his constituents. I come from a riding, Burin-St. George's on the south coast of Newfoundland, that has seen many years of great hardship and many years of great anxiety as a result of the difficulties of a very fragile fishing industry. I can sympathize with my hon. friend and I can sympathize with the problems in the textile industry that he is so concerned about. 1 can assure him that I, as a Member of the House, do indeed understand his comments and concerns.
I am sure that he would agree that the adjustment issues that he refers to are not new only to his riding but indeed are relevant to all of Canada. What we do have to ensure is that our capacity to grow and prosper as a nation goes hand in hand with our ability to manage the attendant changes with care and sensitivity.
As you know, we are living through a difficult transition period brought about by many factors, including international competition and rapid technological change. The challenge is to manage this process in a way to ensure that the benefits and costs of economic adjustment are shared in a fair and equitable manner. In this regard, the Federal Labour Adjustment Benefits Program plays an important role in assisting those who are most adversely affected by plant closures and job loss, namely older workers with a long employment history in a designated industry and with little prospect of re-employment.
The Labour Adjustment Benefits Program provides payments to assist older workers who have been laid off as a result of import competition, industrial restructuring or severe economic disruption in a designated industry and/or region. The program provides last resort income maintenance benefits and is targeted to older workers who have exhausted their unemployment insurance entitlement and are generally not well suited to other adjustment programs. They are not readily employable in other industries or occupations because of their
Textile Industry
age and because their skills are usually specific to the industry from which they have been laid off.
In order to appreciate the intent of the program and its limitations, I would like to provide some background for the record. Labour Canada has maintained an adjustment assistance program since 1972. The program, initially referred to as the Adjustment Assistance Benefits Program, provided benefits to qualified individuals who have been laid off from the textile and clothing industries. This program was extended to workers in the footwear and tanning industries in 1978. Also in 1978, a total review of all Government adjustment measures was undertaken, resulting in the establishment of the Industry and Labour Adjustment Program, more commonly known as ILAP, in 1981.
The Labour Adjustment Benefits Act, promulgated on May 1, 1982, was created to include labour adjustment benefits as part of the ILAP program and to provide for a continuation of benefits from the four general designated industries; textiles, clothing, footwear and tanning. Other industries can be designated either generally or regionally, but to date, only the above-mentioned four industries have been designated generally.
The Act also provided for the establishment of a Labour Adjustment Review Board; the five-person tripartite board which certifies persons, whose lay-offs meet the criteria under the Act, as being eligible to apply to Employment and Immigration for benefits. The following are criteria for certification: the lay-off must have taken place in a designated industry and/or region within the time frame stipulated by the relevant order under the Labour Adjustment Benefits Act; the lay-offs must have been part of a workforce reduction of 10 per cent or 50 employees, which ever is less, within a 12 month period; the workforce reduction must have been caused by one or more of the economic factors causing the designation to be created.
The board's secretariat receives applications, investigates the circumstances and reports and makes recommendations to the board which then renders certification decisions. Qualification of certified individuals to receive Labour Adjustment Benefits is carried out by Employment and Immigration upon receipt of applications from the secretariat.
I think at this point it would be useful to note the conditions under which certified persons may receive benefits. They must be Canadian citizens resident in Canada. They must have worked 1,000 hours in each of 10 of the last 15 years in the relevant designated industry. They must be at least 54 years old at the time of the lay-off and not more than 65 years old. In cases of extreme financial hardship, a person may also qualify if their age and years of service at the time of lay-off add up to 80 years. Their unemployment insurance entitlement must be exhausted and they must have no present prospect of employment or have accepted employment that pays less than the average weekly insurable earnings before lay-off.
Benefits are payable until age 65 and are approximately equal to the unemployment insurance benefits. Benefits are administered by Employment and Immigration, which is then reimbursed by Labour Canada. Policy and designation recom-

mendations are developed by the policy program of Labour Canada. In the case of regional designations, Labour Canada works in close conjunction with Employment and Immigration.
Hon. Members may recall that on April 10, 1984, the Cabinet approved the creation of a modified version of the Industry and Labour Adjustment Program. This program, administered jointly by the Canada Employment and Immigration Commission and Labour Canada, serves as a means of providing emergency assistance to communities experiencing severe economic difficulties of a structural nature resulting in serious disruption of employment.
As the financial resources of the modified Industry and Labour Adjustment Program are limited only the most severely affected communities, which meet the strict criteria of the program can be designated.
The modified ILAP provides two levels of assistance. Workers laid off in communities designated Level 1 are eligible for supplementary job creation measures, training and mobility assistance and CEIC portable wage subsidies. Designation at Level 2 of the program are made in accordance with the Labour Adjustment Benefits Act. In addition to CEIC adjustment measures, older workers laid off in designated industries in communities designated Level 2 are eligible for labour adjustment benefits.
A detailed review of the economic situation of some 240 communities throughout Canada have been made in connection with the modified ILAP. Following this review, the Cabinet on June 21, 1984, announced nine designations of communities most severely affected by massive and permanent lay-offs. Five of these nine designations were at Level 1 of the modified ILAP. These five Level 1 designations were to communities in Newfoundland, Quebec and British Columbia. Three additional designations have subsequently been made, one in Nova Scotia, one other in Newfoundland and an additional one in British Columbia.
Four communities have been designated Level 2 under the modified ILAP. These four communities are located in eastern Quebec and Labrador, and are totally dependent on the iron ore and asbestos industries.
All workers laid off in these designated communities can benefit from CEIC active adjustment measures. In addition to these measures, as I stated, older workers laid off by regional key industries designated under the Labour Adjustment Benefits Act can apply for labour adjustment benefits if they meet the criteria for eligibility.
As far as certification is concerned, the Labour Adjustment Review Board is authorized to grant certification where certain conditions, as outlined in Section 2 of the Act, have been met.
First, the employee must have been laid off. The legislation stipulates that the lay-offs must have taken place in order for certification to be granted. Although lay-offs may be scheduled for a specific date, for example, in a plant closing, the
Labour Adjustment Review Board is not empowered to grant certification nor to provide assessments as to whether certification will be granted in advance of the lay-offs.
Second, the establishment where the lay-offs took place must be part of a designated industry. The determination of whether a company is part of a designated industry is made by the Labour Adjustment Review Board, taking into account the effective dates of designation for the industry.
In the case of general designations, that is the textile, clothing, footwear and tanning industries, there are limitations on the components of the industries which are considered to be designated. These limitations are based on industry definitions, and in this context the board generally refers to the standard industrial classification codes describing the major industry groupings.
In the case of regional designations, the specific industries included are based on Cabinet decisions. Again the board refers to the applicable standard industrial classification codes. Industries can be designated retroactively, Mr. Speaker, and lay-offs which have taken place since the retroactive date of designation may be considered for certification. All existing general designations are retroactive to May 1. 1978.
To determine that the lay-off is within a designated industry and that it meets other requirements of the Act, the secretariat of the Labour Adjustment Review Board carries out a detailed review of the case on behalf of the Board. Notwithstanding that an industry is no longer designated, an employee may be certified provided that the lay-off took place while the industry was designated.
The third condition for granting certification requires that the number of employees in the establishment must have been reduced as a result of lay-offs in any 12 month period by at least 10 per cent or 50 employees, whichever is less. This criterion is designed to ensure that the intent of the legislation is maintained, that is, to offer adjustment assistance where major lay-offs have taken place and where such lay-offs are of a non-cyclical nature.
Since a reduction in the number of employees as a result of lay-offs is a necessary condition for certification, laid-off employees who have been replaced will not be eligible for certification. In cases where lay-offs are taking place but, because of recalls and new hiring, the employee level in a company is stable or rising, certification cannot be granted.
Should lay-offs in the order of 10 per cent take place during part of a 12 month period, additional employees laid off in the remainder of that 12 month period can be certified only where a further reduction in the number of employees is evident and where the other requirements of certification have been met. In considering lay-offs which have taken place during a second 12 month period, it is necessary to establish that the full requirements for certification have been met in relation to the new period. Reduction in the number of employees in an establishment due to retirements, dismissals or resignations cannot be taken into account when determining whether a reduction of 10 per cent or 50 employees has taken place.

The last condition for certification, which I want to mention, is that the lay-offs must have resulted from the economic adjustment which caused the industry to be designated. In the case of general designations, economic adjustment must be non-cyclical and must be the result of import competition or industrial restructuring including technological change pursuant to a policy or program of the Government of Canada.
In the case of regional designations, economic adjustment refers to the serious non-cyclical downturn in the industry causing economic disruption in the region and serious loss of employment in the region.
In conclusion, I would like to emphasize that the Government's financial commitment, while limited, has increased significantly for this fiscal year. For 1985-86 the estimated funds are $20 million more than the amount in 1984-85, almost double the amount allocated last year. This is due to a significant increase in lay-offs in the textile and clothing industries in the Province of Quebec, and in response to the needs of workers in particular industries that have been designated on a regional basis.
I should also like to bring to the attention of the Hon. Member for Drummond that this amount represents the largest allocation of funds in Labour Canada's 1985-86 estimates. That is a very significant point indeed.

I want to assure the Hon. Member that his representations have been heard, are being listened to and are appreciated. As I have mentioned before, I have an industry, unfortunately an industry not designated under the Act, namely the fishing industry, and several references have been made in the House over the last couple of days with respect to that industry. Very few people have indicated that although the fishing industry has not been designated under the Labour Adjustment Benefits Act, Governments-this Government in particular-have responded to the needs of the industry by injecting additional new equity into a company called FBI of Newfoundland. As a result, that industry should now be in a position not only to stabilize but for the first time in five years show a profit. That is a Government responding to the needs of people.
I would like to thank the Hon. Member for Drummond for his representations and for giving me an opportunity to address it on behalf of the Government.
